title: Carney Says Canada and US Making Progress Toward Trade Deal, No Agreement Yet
excerpt: Speaking in Manila, Carney described a long call with President Trump and said a bilateral deal is possible — but Ottawa will not accept terms inconsistent with a viable Canadian auto sector.
body:
• Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada and the United States are making progress toward a bilateral trade deal, but have not reached an agreement.
  • Carney said he held a long, substantive conversation with President Donald Trump, with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and chief of staff Stephen Miller also on the call.
  • Ottawa's stated condition is the auto sector: Carney said his government will not settle for a deal inconsistent with a viable Canadian auto sector.
  • Carney sees a bilateral deal scaling back U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos — a 25 per cent U.S. tariff on Canadian-made autos is part of the current backdrop.

Canada and the United States are making progress toward a trade deal but have not reached one, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Saturday in Manila. Carney told reporters he had held a long, substantive conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump before leaving on his current trip, according to Reuters and The Canadian Press.

"We are making progress. There is the possibility of a bilateral deal, but we are not there yet."

— Mark Carney, Prime Minister of Canada

Carney said U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller were also on the call. He made the remarks in the Philippines, where he is on a state visit and meeting Southeast Asian leaders, when asked about the future of Canada's auto industry following the sale of Stellantis's assembly plant in Brampton, The Canadian Press reported.

Autos are the stated sticking point

Carney framed the auto sector as a condition, not a detail. "This government will not settle for a deal with the United States that is not consistent with a viable Canadian auto sector," he said, according to The Canadian Press.

Reporting summarised by The Brief from The Globe and Mail's coverage adds the tariff context: Carney called the auto talks one of the most challenging issues in the negotiations, said Canada is making headway on terms that would leave a path to profitability for Canadian auto production, and said he sees a bilateral deal scaling back U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos. The backdrop is a 25 per cent U.S. tariff on Canadian-made autos, applying with an exemption for U.S. parts in the vehicles, and the value of Canadian passenger car and light truck exports to the United States fell nearly 12 per cent from 2024 to 2025, The Brief reported.

Carney also argued that the longer-term competitiveness of the U.S. auto sector is partly determined by how closely it is integrated with the Canadian auto sector — the case Ottawa is making for why a deal that damages Canadian production would not serve Washington either.

Progress claimed, terms not disclosed

Neither side has published draft terms, tariff schedules or a timetable. What Carney described on Saturday is movement in talks at leader level, with the central sectoral dispute — autos — still unresolved by his own account. Markets and the North American auto supply chain therefore have a signal of direction, not a deal to price.

Reuters also reported that Carney said Canada would not walk away from NATO, and that the security architecture for a free Europe would be determined by a free Europe and NATO, not Russia.

Canada advances Asian deals in parallel

The trade comments came as Carney announced that Canada and the Philippines had successfully concluded a free trade agreement. At a joint signing ceremony with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Carney said he expects trade between the two countries to triple over the course of the next decade, according to The Canadian Press.

Carney also announced that negotiations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations on a broader trade pact have been substantially completed. "ASEAN brings together 11 countries, 700 million people with a combined economy worth about $6 trillion," he said. The parallel Asian agreements underline Ottawa's stated push to diversify trade while the U.S. negotiation continues.

What to watch next

The next test is whether the leader-level conversation produces negotiator-level text — in particular, any agreed treatment of auto tariffs and of steel and aluminum. Until terms are published, Carney's position as stated on Saturday is the only firm guide: progress, a possible bilateral deal, and no agreement that leaves the Canadian auto sector unviable.
